\chapter{Asking Well}
\label{ch:ml-asking-well}
\hlchaptermodality{65}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a request, permission, consent, good manners and trust in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C65-trust and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[apēkṣa]{\ml{അപേക്ഷ} (apēkṣa) — a request}

\label{lesson:ML-C65-request}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{mātraṁ} mean, and what did \emph{ennāl} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അപേക്ഷ}}
\textbf{\ml{അപേക്ഷ}} (\emph{apēkṣa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a request\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{apekṣā}, made of a piece meaning toward and a root meaning to look. A request is a looking-toward: the eyes go to the person who can grant it before the words do.

It carries the \ml{ക്ഷ} pair you have now met twice, in \emph{kṣamikkaṇaṁ} and in \emph{kṣīṇaṁ}, this time sitting in the middle of the word rather than at its head.

Beside \emph{dayavāyi}, which softens whatever follows it, \ml{അപേക്ഷ} names the asking itself and can stand on its own at the head of a written petition.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for asking well.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{apēkṣa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dayavāyi}, then \emph{apēkṣa}, and say which of the two is the asking itself
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{അപേക്ഷ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a request\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anuvādaṁ]{\ml{അനുവാദം} (anuvādaṁ) — permission}

\label{lesson:ML-C65-permission}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{apēkṣa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അനുവാദം}}
\textbf{\ml{അനുവാദം}} (\emph{anuvādaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{anuvāda}: a piece meaning after or along, and a piece meaning speaking. Permission is the speaking-after, the second voice that falls in behind the first.

The same Sanskrit word names a repetition and a translation, which is one picture seen from another side — saying again what somebody else has already said.

So the shape of the courtesy is built into the word: somebody asks, and somebody speaks after.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anuvādaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{apēkṣa}, then \emph{anuvādaṁ}, and say which one comes first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{അനുവാദം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sammataṁ]{\ml{സമ്മതം} (sammataṁ) — consent, an agreeing}

\label{lesson:ML-C65-consent}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{anuvādaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{സമ്മതം}}
\textbf{\ml{സമ്മതം}} (\emph{sammataṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}consent, an agreeing\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{sammata}: a piece meaning together, and \emph{mata}, a thought held. Consent is two minds held in one position.

That \emph{mata} piece stands behind the Sanskrit word for an opinion and for a doctrine, so what a household calls agreement and what a school of thought calls its position are the same word wearing different clothes.

Between the two you now have, \emph{anuvādaṁ} comes down from somebody with the standing to grant it and \ml{സമ്മതം} passes sideways between equals.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sammataṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{anuvādaṁ}, then \emph{sammataṁ}, and say which of the two is given from above
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{സമ്മതം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}consent, an agreeing\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maryāda]{\ml{മര്യാദ} (maryāda) — good manners}

\label{lesson:ML-C65-manners}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sammataṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മര്യാദ}}
\textbf{\ml{മര്യാദ}} (\emph{maryāda}) — \textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{maryādā}, whose first sense was a boundary mark set at the edge of a field, and whose second is the bounds of proper conduct.

Kerala keeps both senses live in one word. To have \ml{മര്യാദ} is to know where the edges are and to stop at them without being asked.

Beside \emph{bahumānaṁ}, respect, which is something a person shows another, this is something a person keeps for themselves.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maryāda}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bahumānaṁ}, then \emph{maryāda}, and say which of the two you show and which you keep
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മര്യാദ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viśvāsaṁ]{\ml{വിശ്വാസം} (viśvāsaṁ) — trust}

\label{lesson:ML-C65-trust}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maryāda} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വിശ്വാസം}}
\textbf{\ml{വിശ്വാസം}} (\emph{viśvāsaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{viśvāsa}, from a root about breathing. Trust is drawn there as breathing out — a body that has stopped holding itself ready.

The same root sits behind the Sanskrit word for a sigh, which is the same picture again, and the metaphor survives whole into everyday Malayalam.

It also carries belief in the religious sense, so the everyday and the weightier senses share a word and the situation says which is meant.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and asking has its vocabulary: a request, permission, consent, good manners, and the trust the other four rest on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viśvāsaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{apēkṣa}, \emph{anuvādaṁ}, \emph{sammataṁ}, \emph{maryāda}, \emph{viśvāsaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വിശ്വാസം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
